title: George McCollum, Olympia personnel, trombonists and readers who could play hot
summary: McCollum picking up an unknown tune in Bay St. Louis, Olympia instrumentation, Henry Glass as bass drummer, and whether good readers could swing.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well, let's not leave George McCollum out, Alvin Alcorn. See, as you talk, you think, you see? Think like George McCollum. George McCollum was a, he ain't number one trumpet man, but he was better when you put the music up there too. He was great. I remember one time in Basin, Mississippi, we was playing with Desdun, we was playing the advertisement. George McCollum picked up a number, nobody knew what number and what it was, but it sounds some good. And everybody fell right on in there with him, and the people started dancing in the street and everything. So we was playing in front of this drugstore where every time we go to Basin, we go play in front of this drugstore, the man gives all the seagull. So they asked George, what the devil did you pick up there? Yeah. I said, man, that sounds some good. We never heard of Davenport, George. I said, that's a seagull stomp. Yeah, you just pick up a number. You know, you went to pick up one number and pick up another number. That number ever could have been recorded. I think it would have been, went over big. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, well I think, but covered, but I could talk, I guess a couple hours on good trumpet players, and things, we've got a lot of them around here. We had a lot of them done, still got a lot of them around here. Thomas Jefferson, Joe Phillip, all those good trumpet players. He's playing good again. Howard was sick, but he's getting back like kid Howard one more time. He's living a second life now. If you'd have seen the way he looked when I went to the hospital, you would know what I mean when I say he's living a second life. He lived two lives. He lived one and he's living a second one right now. I don't know. Yeah. Well, in a brass band, I've been using Josiah Freddie, they call him Saeed on snare drum, Henry Glass on bass drum, and when Saeed can't play, well Paul Byrath always take his place. Sometimes the band might use three reeds, cryin' that and two saxons, sometimes one saxon, one cryin' that and three trumpets. They usually carry ten pieces, but every nine in the brass band tries to stick another one in, which is eleven, and I think they ought to carry eleven or twelve pieces all the time, because it would sound a lot better. And another thing I want to mention, we've got a drum player around here, but the only one close to Black Benny's playing is Henry Glass. He's the closest bass drum player to Black Benny. In fact, I think that's where you guys inspiration from. And a long time ago when Black Benny was popular, you had to play it because they had so many good things. Of course they had a lot of good trombone players too in them days, like Sonny Henry, Louis Warner, and when I was playing Rita Tuck City he had a trombone player with him. I never could think of the man's name, but he played some trombone. Were the good readers ever very hot? Were they very hot?
Well, some of them. But you see, a good reader, in them days a good reader looked like when you took a hot chorus, it was a little different, hot, from a man that couldn't read.
In other words, they could get off?

Yeah, sure they could get off. Man Perez could get off pretty good, and he was a good reader. I know him at Twyler, get off a little bit, beautiful, he was a good trumpet player. George McCollum could get off. Leo, he could get off.
